text.p: The European Union, with its 15 member countries and 373 million citizens, is not the centre of the universe, the European Commission confirmed on Tuesday.

"In 1950 the EU made up 12 percent (of world population). It now represents seven percent and...by 2050 it will only account for three percent," Commission spokesman Joao Vale de Almeida told a news conference, citing figures released by the EU's Statistical Office, Eurostat.
By the start of 1996 there were six Chinese and five Indians for every two EU citizens, according to Eurostat's "Beyond the predictable: demographic changes in the EU up to 2050".
Even if Europe sees a boom in migration and birth rates -- now at a historical low of 1.45 children per woman -- the EU's share of global population will continue to fall.
The Eurostat report offers a variety of predictions based on different birth rate, life expectancy and migration scenarios.

The lowest population growth forecast indicates that deaths will outstrip births this year and that even with the expected arrival of a minimum 400,000 new immigrants, the EU's population will have returned by 2050 to its 1950 level of 303 million.

By 2050 the number of elderly people could have doubled to reach 40 percent of Europe's population -- a third of them over 80 years old -- and the number of people under 20 could have fallen by nearly half, from 90 to 52 million.
Europe's working population is likely to go into a long period of decline early next century, unless there is another baby boom and a leap in migration.
But Eurostat has some good news for Europeans concerned about the EU's weight in the world.

European babies born in 2050 could live 20 years longer than generations born in the early twentieth century if, and only if, there are continual improvements in medical care and healthy lifestyles, with life expectancy as high as 87 for girls and 83 for boys.
And in spite of everything, there are still more Europeans than Americans.
